MEETING HEADER
Date: 2026-03-25
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Martin (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Mike Chen (Head of ML, Raven Tech), Sara Lopez (Platform Eng), Tom Rogers (CTO)

SUMMARY:
Quick cost/unit economics intake focused on deciding between Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Key constraints: strict P99 latency target (200ms), budget cap for first year $250k, data residency EU, SOC2 required. Team wants clear unit cost numbers and knobs: batching, KV prefix cache, quantization, routing/fallbacks.

TOPICS:
- Current stack and RPS
- Latency SLO and budget constraints
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
- Batching, caching, quantization levers
- Security/compliance (SOC2, SSO, KMS)
- Next steps (benchmarks, pricing worksheet, pilot)

TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, um let me just share my screen — hope that timing works for you in europe. Alex Martin, AE at Redwood.
[00:15] Mike: yeah thanks Alex, Mike here. we have about 35 minutes set aside, so high level we want to understand how to cost-effectively serve our summarization pipeline, and whether we should go hosted or bring our own.
[00:28] Priya: hi all, Priya, I'm the solutions engineer. quick clarifier, when you say summarization pipeline what's your average prompt length and tokens per request?
[00:38] Mike: so average input about 800 tokens, output around 400 tokens for final summary. we run roughly 50 QPS at peak, bursty during end-of-day. p99 latency around 200 ms is our bar — the product team says no more than 250 but we aim 200.
[00:55] Sara: and security — data must live in eu for now, SOC2 required, sso via okta, kms for keys.
[01:06] Alex: great, that's helpful. budget wise Mike? you gave our SDR a ballpark, want to state it here?
[01:13] Mike: yeah we have a $250k first-year ceiling for inference costs, not including dev costs. we're open to dedicated if it brings predictability.
[01:23] Priya: ok, perfect. i'll walk through cost levers — batching, kv cache, quantization, and routing — and then we can map to hosted/dedicated/private. note: numbers i'll quote are rough, we'll follow up with a pricing worksheet.
[01:38] Alex: just to keep expectations — hosted is faster to get started, dedicated gives committed throughput, private gives the most control for compliance but higher ops.
[01:48] Mike: can you give a concrete unit cost per 1k tokens example?
[01:52] Priya: sure, rough today: hosted with our curated 13B fp16 model at typical batch sizing you might see $0.12–0.18 per 1k tokens. with batching/kv cache improvements that can drop to $0.07–0.1 per 1k. Dedicated (reserved gpus) can push that to $0.04–0.08 per 1k depending on utilization and quantization.
[02:12] Tom: that delta seems big — but is that assuming same latency? our p99 200ms requirement seems tough if you push cost down with large batch windows.
[02:23] Priya: exactly. batching reduces per-token cost but increases tail latency. our runtime does continuous batching and adaptive windows — so you can set SLOs at p99 and we tune batching thresholds. KV prefix cache is another lever — if you have repetitive prefixes we can cache key/value states to skip recomputation for initial tokens which reduces both latency and cost.
[02:45] Sara: curious about quantization — our models are consumer-open models, how much do we lose on quality when going 8-bit or 4-bit for embeddings and generation?
[02:55] Priya: depends on model and tasks. for summarization we often recommend 4-bit quant (Q4) for 13B-class models — small BLEU/ROUGE delta in most internal evals. we can run your eval set; often quality loss is negligible but safe to test. quantization also reduces memory footprint so you can fit more replicas on a GPU which improves throughput/unit cost.
[03:14] Mike: what's the recommended path for budget predictability? we don't want surprising overages.
[03:19] Alex: dedicated reserved capacity gives predictable monthly commit with discounted unit price; hosted can be usage-based and is easier for ramping. we also have hybrid routing so you can start hosted then move steady-state to dedicated while pegging a budget cap for hosted bursts.
[03:37] Tom: and private? if we need VPC/on-prem for compliance — cost and ops tradeoff?
[03:41] Priya: private gives full control — you manage infra and we provide a control plane with observability. more ops burden and usually higher fixed cost. but for strict data residency and compliance it can be preferable. we can share our on-prem packaging checklist.
[03:56] Mike: ok, on tokens and bill lingo — are we billed on consumed tokens or generated tokens? prefix cache changes that math.
[04:03] Priya: our billing is per token processed by the runtime: input + output tokens. with KV/prefix caching, if a token is served from cache we discount billing for the cached portion; we show token-level breakdown in the console so you can trace cost to route or endpoint.
[04:20] Alex: and we provide tooling to estimate monthly spend given request mix — we'll send a worksheet where you can plug your avg input/output tokens, QPS, and target latency to get estimated spend across hosted/dedicated/private.
[04:33] Sara: would love that. can you also show how autoscaling interacts with reserved capacity? our infra team worries about spikes.
[04:40] Priya: reserved pools support burst capacity and autoscaling policies. on Dedicated you set a baseline commit for guaranteed throughput and allow burst to shared capacity or pay-as-you-go for short bursts. we also support fallback routing to a cheaper or higher-capacity model when commit is exhausted.
[04:58] Mike: are there hard p99 guarantees in SLA for dedicated?
[05:02] Alex: we offer SLA-backed uptime and latency targets on Dedicated at enterprise contracts; SLA specifics depend on committed tiers. we can include targets for p99 tail latency in the contract and run joint benchmarks during pilot.
[05:16] Tom: about benchmarks — can you show an apples-to-apples run with our prompt shapes? last vendor did optimistic numbers that didn't match our workload.
[05:23] Priya: absolutely — we prefer running a shadow benchmark with your sample traffic. best practice is a 24–72 hour soak with representative mix. for quicker signals we'll do a 1–2 hour load test for cost and latency snapshot. i'll run a 5000-token synthetic and a 1200-token representative one.
[05:40] Mike: great. what telemetry do you provide? we need token-level cost, per-route latency breakdown, and per-request trace ids.
[05:48] Alex: Redwood Console exposes per-route/model token breakdown, p50/p90/p99 latency histograms, trace hooks, and cost allocation. we can export to your prometheus or datadog, and push logs to your S3/GCS for audits.
[06:01] Sara: and security — SOC2 attestation and okta SSO? we also want KMS integration for keys.
[06:07] Alex: SOC2 Type II is available, we support SAML/OKTA SSO and RBAC, and KMS/HSM integrations for Private and Dedicated. for Hosted we can integrate KMS for customer encryption keys with appropriate agreements.
[06:22] Mike: good. curious about model variants — if we need a faster but cheaper variant how does routing work?
[06:29] Priya: routing policies are flexible: route by latency SLO, cost threshold, region, or tier. automatic fallback can route to a smaller or quantized model on overload. canary and A/B rollouts supported too.
[06:44] Tom: what about tokenization differences across vendors — ensures cost estimates are comparable?
[06:49] Priya: we recommend running your tokenizer on sample inputs in our worksheet. small differences exist but we normalize in the calculator. we'll instrument to compute tokens according to the model's tokenizer.
[06:58] Mike: ok last area: observability during a pilot — how do we verify costs don't blow up mid-pilot?
[07:04] Alex: we set thresholds and alerts, e.g., daily spend cap, per-route token rate alarms, and auto-fallback rules. plus weekly check-ins with a CSM for pilots.
[07:15] Sara: and how long to get a pilot running if we start next week?
[07:19] Alex: hosted pilot can start within 48–72 hours. dedicated pilot setup (reserved pool) is 2–4 weeks, depends on procurement and region capacity. private on-prem takes longer — usually 6–8 weeks.
[07:31] Mike: ok let's summarize next steps.
[07:34] Alex: sure — recap: Alex to send pricing worksheet + quantization playbook; Priya to run quick benchmarks with two payload sizes and KV cache demo; Mike to share sample request set and SLOs; schedule pilot kickoff week of Apr 6. we'll also attach SOC2 and on-prem checklist.
[07:53] Tom: sounds good. any more questions?
[07:56] Sara: none from me.
[07:58] Mike: no, thanks everyone.
[08:00] Alex: thanks all, we'll follow up with docs and the worksheet. bye.
